pos: v. (past tense of speak; rendering Hebrew dabar, Greek elalesen)
etymology: The older strong past tense of speak, from Saxon spræc. Modern English has levelled it to spoke. In the Authorized Version it is the standing verb of revelation: the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, a formula repeated well over a hundred times in the Pentateuch alone.
biblical_def: Spake is the old past of speak, and its repetition in the Authorized Version is one of the plainest evidences of what Scripture claims for itself. “And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying” (Leviticus 7:22, and scores of places besides) is not a literary refrain but a claim about the origin of the words that follow: they were spoken, by a Person, to a named man, at a place. The same formula opens God's dealing with Noah after the flood: “And God spake unto Noah, and to his sons with him, saying” (Genesis 9:8). Isaiah records the manner as well as the fact: “For the LORD spake thus to me with a strong hand, and instructed me that I should not walk in the way of this people” (Isaiah 8:11) — a compulsion the prophet felt as pressure, setting him against the whole current of his nation. And the Gospels use it of Christ's own speech, often before a hostile audience: “Jesus answering spake unto the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day?” (Luke 14:3).
webster_summary: The older past tense of speak, now levelled to spoke. In Scripture it is the verb of revelation — the LORD spake unto Moses, God spake unto Noah — asserting that the words following were actually spoken by God to a named man.
webster_full: SPAKE, v. [Sax. spræc.] The past tense of speak; now more commonly spoke.
2. To utter words; to express thoughts by words; to talk.
3. To deliver a message or a command; as, the LORD spake unto Moses.
4. It belongs to the class of strong verbs, which form the past by an internal vowel change.
5. In Scripture, And God spake unto Noah, Gen. 9; the LORD spake thus to me with a strong hand, Isa. 8.
corruption_summary: The verbal inspiration of Scripture is regularly reduced to a claim that the writers had religious experiences and reported them. The formula the LORD spake claims something stronger: God spoke words, and the words were written down.
corruption_paragraphs: Historical-critical scholarship has largely treated these formulae as later editorial framing, the work of redactors imposing divine authority on collected traditions. The documentary hypothesis divides the Pentateuch among hypothetical sources and assigns the legal material to a Priestly hand centuries after Moses; on that reading, the LORD spake unto Moses is a literary convention rather than a report. The dictionary rejects this. Mosaic authorship is the position of the text itself, of the later prophets, and of Christ, who spoke of Moses as the author and treated the words as God's.

What is at stake is verbal plenary inspiration — that God so superintended the writers that the words they produced are His words, without destroying their own style or personality. Peter states the mechanism: prophecy came not in old time by the will of man, but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. Isaiah 8:11 lets us feel it from inside: the LORD spake with a strong hand, and the prophet found himself instructed against the way of his own people. That is neither dictation of an unwilling scribe nor mere religious insight; it is a man overmastered and speaking truly.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar is to speak, and its noun dabar means both word and thing; 'amar is to say. Greek uses laleo for the act of speaking and lego for the content spoken.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1696) — to speak, to declare; the verb of the formula the LORD spake unto Moses.
Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter, a thing; the noun from the same root, uniting speech and reality.
Greek laleo (G2980) — to speak, to utter; its aorist elalesen renders the Hebrew formula.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, to carry; in 2 Peter 1:21 holy men were moved, borne along, by the Holy Ghost.
Saxon spræc — the Old English past of sprecan, to speak; source of spake.
usage: Of God addressing Noah after the flood: And God spake unto Noah, and to his sons with him, saying (Genesis 9:8).
Of the standing formula of the law: And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying (Leviticus 7:22).
Of a prophet set against his own nation: the LORD spake thus to me with a strong hand (Isaiah 8:11).

pos: v. (past tense of break; rendering Hebrew shabar, Greek eklasen)
etymology: The older strong past tense of break, from Saxon bræc; modern English has levelled it to broke. Distinguish the noun brake, a thicket or a fern, which is a separate word.
biblical_def: Brake is the old past of break, and Scripture uses it for three kinds of breaking. The first is the breaking of bread at the institution of the Lord's Supper: “Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body” (Matthew 26:26), and in Luke with the added charge, “this do in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). The breaking is not incidental. It is a sign, and the church has kept the action ever since. The second is the breaking down of idols in reformation: Josiah “brake in pieces the images, and cut down the groves, and filled their places with the bones of men” (2 Kings 23:14) — a thorough work, defiling the sites so that they could not be quietly restored. The third is judgment: “he called for a famine upon the land: he brake the whole staff of bread” (Psalm 105:16), and the Chaldeans who “brake down the walls of Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 39:8). And Exodus records a breaking that led to idolatry rather than away from it, when the people “brake off the golden earrings which were in their ears” for Aaron to melt.
webster_summary: The older past tense of break, now levelled to broke. In Scripture it marks the breaking of bread at the Lord's Supper, the breaking down of idols in reformation, and the breaking of the staff of bread in judgment.
webster_full: BRAKE, v. [Sax. bræc.] The past tense of break; now more commonly broke.
2. To part or divide by force; to sever; to shatter.
3. To destroy or demolish, as an image or a wall.
4. BRAKE, n. A place overgrown with fern or brambles; a thicket. A distinct word.
5. In Scripture, blessed it, and brake it, Matt. 26; he brake in pieces the images, 2 Kings 23.
corruption_summary: The breaking of bread is corrupted at both extremes: by transubstantiation, which makes the elements cease to be bread, and by a bare memorialism that makes the Supper nothing but a mental exercise. The Reformed position holds the sign and the spiritual reality together.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome teaches that the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ, the appearances alone remaining, and that the mass is a propitiatory sacrifice offered again. Scripture forbids both halves. Christ was bodily present holding the bread when He said this is my body, so the words cannot mean what Trent requires; and Hebrews insists that His one offering was made once for all, after which He sat down — a sacrifice repeated is a sacrifice unfinished. The Lutheran doctrine of a bodily presence in, with, and under the elements is rejected on the same Christological grounds.

But the opposite error is common among Baptists and does real damage. A bare Zwinglian memorialism reduces the Supper to a remembering, with nothing given and nothing received, and congregations that hold it tend to observe the ordinance rarely and thinly. The 1689 Confession teaches otherwise: worthy receivers, outwardly partaking of the visible elements, do then also inwardly by faith really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified. The bread is bread; Christ is truly given to faith; and the breaking is a sign that means something because a body really was broken.
roots_summary: Hebrew shabar is to break or shatter, used of vessels, of images, and of the staff of bread; Greek klao is to break, and gives klasis artou, the breaking of bread, the earliest name for the Supper.
roots_lines: Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break, shatter, burst; used of idols, walls, and the staff of bread.
Hebrew matteh lechem (H4294, H3899) — the staff of bread; the support that famine breaks in Psalm 105:16.
Greek klao (G2806) — to break; its aorist eklasen is used of Christ at the institution.
Greek klasis (G2800) — a breaking; the breaking of bread in Acts 2:42, an early name for the Supper.
Saxon bræc — the Old English past of brecan, to break.
usage: Of the institution of the Lord's Supper: blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples (Matthew 26:26).
Of thorough reformation against idols: he brake in pieces the images, and cut down the groves (2 Kings 23:14).
Of famine sent as judgment: he brake the whole staff of bread (Psalm 105:16).

pos: v. (past tense of cleave; rendering Hebrew dabaq and baqa', Greek kollao)
etymology: The past tense of cleave — but English has two verbs of that spelling with opposite senses. One means to stick fast (Saxon cleofian), the other to split apart (Saxon cleofan), and the Authorized Version uses clave for both. Hebrew keeps them distinct: dabaq to cling, baqa' to cleave asunder.
biblical_def: Clave is the past of two opposite verbs, and Scripture uses both. In the sense of clinging it describes the strongest attachments in the Bible. Ruth's decision is stated in one clause: “Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her” (Ruth 1:14) — the kiss and the cleaving set side by side, affection against covenant loyalty. Hezekiah's reign is summarised the same way: “he clave to the LORD, and departed not from following him, but kept his commandments” (2 Kings 18:6). The word is the same one used in Genesis 2:24 of a man cleaving unto his wife, which is why Shechem's case is so pointed: his soul “clave unto Dinah” (Genesis 34:3) after he had violated her, the right word for a relation begun the wrong way. In the sense of splitting, the ground “clave asunder” under Korah (Numbers 16:31), and God “clave the rocks in the wilderness” to give His people drink (Psalm 78:15). At Athens, after mockery from most, “certain men clave unto him, and believed” (Acts 17:34).
webster_summary: The past tense of cleave, a word that in English carries two opposite senses: to stick fast, and to split apart. In Scripture Ruth clave unto Naomi and Hezekiah clave to the LORD, while the ground clave asunder under Korah.
webster_full: CLAVE, v. The past tense of cleave. Two distinct verbs share this form.
2. CLEAVE, v.i. [Sax. cleofian.] To stick; to adhere; to hold to; as, a man shall cleave unto his wife.
3. CLEAVE, v.t. [Sax. cleofan.] To part or divide by force; to split; as, he clave the rocks.
4. The Hebrew keeps the two senses in separate roots, dabaq and baqa'.
5. In Scripture, but Ruth clave unto her, Ruth 1; he clave to the LORD, 2 Kings 18.
corruption_summary: The cleaving that Genesis 2:24 requires of a husband — leaving father and mother and holding fast to one woman — has been reduced to a feeling that may pass. Scripture makes it an act of the will, sworn before God, and the word for it is the same word used of a man's loyalty to the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: That dabaq serves both for a husband cleaving to his wife and for Hezekiah cleaving to the LORD is not an accident of vocabulary. Marriage in Scripture is covenantal in the same sense that Israel's bond to God is covenantal: entered by oath, sealed by a sign, and kept whether or not it remains agreeable. Ephesians makes the parallel explicit, quoting Genesis 2:24 and calling it a great mystery concerning Christ and the church. Where marriage is reduced to a contract of mutual satisfaction, the figure it was made to carry is lost along with the institution.

The Shechem narrative in Genesis 34 is placed exactly to prevent a sentimental reading. Shechem's soul clave unto Dinah, and he loved her, and he spake kindly to her — after he had taken her by force. Scripture reports the affection without excusing the crime, and the chapter goes on to record a revenge that it likewise reports without commending, Jacob condemning his sons for it on his deathbed. Genuine cleaving begins in covenant and not in desire; where desire runs ahead of covenant, the whole story goes wrong, and Genesis 34 is the case study.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabaq means to cling, adhere, or be joined; baqa' means to split or cleave asunder. Greek uses kollao (to glue, to join) for the first sense and schizo for the second.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabaq (H1692) — to cling, cleave, keep close; used of husband and wife, and of a man and the LORD.
Hebrew baqa' (H1234) — to split, cleave open, break through; used of the ground under Korah and of the rock in the wilderness.
Greek kollao (G2853) — to glue or cement together; the New Testament word for cleaving to a person or a thing.
Greek proskollao (G4347) — to join fast to; the verb in the citation of Genesis 2:24 in Ephesians 5:31.
Saxon cleofian and cleofan — the two Old English verbs, to adhere and to split, which fell together in English.
usage: Of covenant loyalty chosen over a parting kiss: Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her (Ruth 1:14).
Of a king's steadfastness summarised: he clave to the LORD, and departed not from following him (2 Kings 18:6).
Of the earth splitting under judgment: the ground clave asunder that was under them (Numbers 16:31).

And they lifted up their voice, and wept again: and Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her.
2 Kings 18:6

Numbers 16:31
And it came to pass, as he had made an end of speaking all these words, that the ground clave asunder that was under them:
Acts 17:34

pos: v. (past tense of swear; rendering Hebrew shaba', Greek omosen)
etymology: The older strong past tense of swear, from Saxon swor; modern English has levelled it to swore. Hebrew shaba' is built on the number seven, and to swear was literally to seven oneself — the sacred number invoked in the binding of a promise.
biblical_def: Sware is the old past of swear, and Scripture uses it of oaths between men and, more weightily, of God's own oath. Abraham and Abimelech settle a dispute over a well and name the place for what happened there: “he called that place Beersheba; because there they sware both of them” (Genesis 21:31). Jacob binds Joseph about his burial (Genesis 47:31). David, who could have destroyed Saul in the cave, instead swears to spare his house: “And David sware unto Saul” (1 Samuel 24:22). Asa's reformation is sealed by a national oath taken aloud: “they sware unto the LORD with a loud voice, and with shouting, and with trumpets, and with cornets” (2 Chronicles 15:14). But the most consequential oaths in Scripture are God's. He swore to the fathers to give the land; He swore in His wrath that a generation should not enter His rest (Numbers 32:10); and He swore by Himself to Abraham, because He could swear by no greater — which is the argument of Hebrews 6 for the immutability of His counsel.
webster_summary: The older past tense of swear, now levelled to swore. In Scripture it records oaths between men — at Beersheba, in the cave, at Asa's reformation — and above all the oath of God, who swore by Himself because He could swear by no greater.
webster_full: SWARE, v. [Sax. swor.] The past tense of swear; now more commonly swore.
2. To affirm or promise with a solemn appeal to God for the truth of the declaration.
3. To bind oneself by oath; as, David sware unto Saul.
4. The Hebrew shaba' is from sheba', seven; to swear was to seven oneself, invoking the sacred number.
5. In Scripture, there they sware both of them, Gen. 21; they sware unto the LORD with a loud voice, 2 Chron. 15.
corruption_summary: God's oath is sometimes treated as a mere figure of speech, since God cannot lie and therefore needs no oath. Hebrews takes it the other way: the oath was added not because His word required support but because our weakness required comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the ground of assurance in God's sworn promise. Hebrews 6 reasons that men swear by the greater, and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife; wherefore God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of His counsel, confirmed it by an oath. Two immutable things follow — the promise and the oath — in both of which it was impossible for God to lie. The doubling is not for God's sake but for ours, that we might have strong consolation.

The same passage rebukes an assurance sought elsewhere. Believers commonly look for confidence in the strength of their own believing, and so rise and fall with their frames. The anchor Hebrews describes is fixed within the veil, where the forerunner is for us entered; it is Christ's presence there and God's sworn word that hold, not the vigour of the grip. Numbers 32:10 shows the other edge of the same attribute: God also swears in wrath, and what He swears then is equally unalterable. An oath from God settles a matter permanently in whichever direction it points.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaba', to swear, derives from sheba', seven; hence Beersheba, the well of the oath or of seven. Greek omnuo is to swear, and horkos is the oath itself.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaba' (H7650) — to swear, to adjure; literally to seven oneself, to bind by the sacred number.
Hebrew sheba' (H7651) — seven; the root behind both swearing and the name Beersheba.
Greek omnuo (G3660) — to swear, to take an oath; its aorist omosen is used of God in Hebrews 6:13.
Greek horkos (G3727) — an oath; that which confirms a promise and ends strife among men.
Saxon swor — the Old English past of swerian, to swear.
usage: Of an oath that named a place: he called that place Beersheba; because there they sware both of them (Genesis 21:31).
Of mercy sworn to an enemy: And David sware unto Saul (1 Samuel 24:22).
Of a national covenant renewed aloud: they sware unto the LORD with a loud voice (2 Chronicles 15:14).

pos: v. (past tense of smite; rendering Hebrew nakah, Greek epataxen)
etymology: The past tense of smite, from Saxon smitan, to strike. The verb survives in English chiefly through the Authorized Version, and it covers everything from a blow of the hand to the destruction of an army, from a plague to the striking of a conscience.
biblical_def: Smote is the past of smite, to strike, and Hebrew nakah ranges across every degree of the action. It records the ordinary language of ancient warfare: “Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword” (Joshua 11:10); “David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah” (2 Samuel 8:3). It records the plagues on Egypt: “He smote their vines also and their fig trees; and brake the trees of their coasts” (Psalm 105:33). And in one of the smallest and sharpest uses in Scripture, it records God's dealing with a prophet's comfort: “God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered” (Jonah 4:7). The whole force of Jonah's book turns on that verse. God, who had spared a city of six-score thousand persons, takes away one plant, and the prophet who begrudged mercy to Nineveh grieves bitterly for a gourd he neither made nor tended.
webster_summary: The past tense of smite, to strike; used of blows, of battle, of plague, and of God's direct action. In Scripture it ranges from the smiting of kings and armies to the worm that smote Jonah's gourd.
webster_full: SMOTE, v. [Sax. smitan.] The past tense of smite; to have struck.
2. To strike with the hand, a weapon, or an instrument; to give a blow to.
3. To kill; to destroy the life of, by a weapon or by a stroke.
4. To afflict; to chasten; to punish; as, God smote the land with a plague.
5. In Scripture, smote the king thereof with the sword, Josh. 11; it smote the gourd that it withered, Jonah 4.
corruption_summary: The conquest narratives are treated by modern readers either as an embarrassment to be explained away or as a licence for present-day violence. Both misread them: they record a unique judicial act of God against specific nations, executed by a covenant people under direct command, and never repeated.
corruption_paragraphs: The moral objection assumes the Canaanites were dispossessed arbitrarily. Scripture says otherwise and says it early: God tells Abraham that his descendants will not return for four generations, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full — four centuries of forbearance before judgment. Leviticus 18 catalogues the practices for which the land spued out its inhabitants, including the burning of children, and warns Israel in the same breath that the land will do the same to her. That warning was executed: Israel herself was smitten and exiled for the same offences. The conquest is judgment, not ethnic preference.

The abuse in the other direction is more urgent, because it is not merely academic. No nation, army, or movement today holds the commission Joshua held. The conquest was a unique, bounded, divinely commanded act within redemptive history, and the New Testament transfers the warfare entirely: our weapons are not carnal, and the sword the church wields is the word of God. The magistrate bears a real sword under Romans 13, for the punishment of evildoers within his own sphere, and that is a different thing altogether. Anyone reasoning from Joshua 11 to a present-day campaign has misread both testaments.
roots_summary: Hebrew nakah covers the whole range of striking — a blow, a wound, a defeat, a plague. Greek patasso is to strike or smite, used of the shepherd smitten in Zechariah's prophecy and of the angel striking Herod.
roots_lines: Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to strike, smite, wound, kill; the single verb behind nearly every English smote.
Hebrew maggephah (H4046) — a plague or slaughter; the noun of the same root, of God's striking.
Greek patasso (G3960) — to strike, smite; used in I will smite the shepherd, quoted by Christ.
Hebrew qiqayon (H7021) — the gourd or plant prepared for Jonah and then smitten by the worm.
Saxon smitan — to strike, to smear; the root of the English verb.
usage: Of the conquest under Joshua: took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword (Joshua 11:10).
Of the plagues upon Egypt: He smote their vines also and their fig trees (Psalm 105:33).
Of a prophet's comfort taken away to teach him mercy: it smote the gourd that it withered (Jonah 4:7).

pos: v. (past tense of beget; rendering Hebrew yalad in the causative, Greek egennesen)
etymology: The past tense of beget, from Saxon begitan, to obtain or procreate. It is the verb of the genealogies, and its monotonous repetition through Genesis, Chronicles, and Matthew 1 is the load-bearing structure of the whole biblical narrative.
biblical_def: Begat is the verb of the genealogies, and the genealogies are not filler. They are the record of a promise carried through history by particular men in a particular line. Genesis begins the tracking almost immediately — “Irad begat Mehujael: and Mehujael begat Methusael: and Methusael begat Lamech” (Genesis 4:18) — and the two lines of Cain and Seth run in parallel to show what each produced. The word marks the entrance of a tyrant: “Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth” (Genesis 10:8). It marks the arrival of the man through whom the whole promise would run: “Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran” (Genesis 11:26). Chronicles rehearses the lines again after the exile, when the question of who belonged to Israel was urgent, and Matthew opens the New Testament with the same verb, tracing the generations from Abraham to David and from David to Christ. The repetition is the argument: God keeps promises across centuries, through named men, most of them obscure.
webster_summary: The past tense of beget, to procreate as the father. It is the verb of the biblical genealogies, whose repetition traces the promise from Adam through Abraham and David to Christ, through named men across many centuries.
webster_full: BEGAT, v. [Sax. begitan.] The past tense of beget; to have procreated as the father.
2. To generate; to produce, as a father produces a child.
3. Figuratively, to produce as an effect; as, luxury begets vice.
4. The Hebrew yalad in the causative stem, to cause to bear, gives the toledoth, the generations.
5. In Scripture, Cush begat Nimrod, Gen. 10; Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Gen. 11.
corruption_summary: The genealogies are commonly skipped as tedious or dismissed as later fabrications. They are neither: they are the historical spine of redemption, and they assume throughout the historicity of the men they name, beginning with Adam.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal depends on whether these lists record real men. Luke traces the descent of Christ back through David and Abraham to Adam, the son of God, without any change of register that would signal a shift from history to legend. Paul's argument in Romans 5 requires a historical Adam, since the whole parallel of one man's disobedience and one Man's obedience collapses if the first is a symbol and the second a person. The dictionary holds a historical Adam and Eve as the first parents of all humanity, and the genealogies are among the reasons.

The lists also carry a doctrine of ordinary faithfulness. Between Abraham and David, and between David and Christ, stand dozens of men of whom nothing is recorded but that they lived and had sons. Some were wicked; Matthew's list includes Manasseh and passes through Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Uriah. God's promise ran through that line without being purified of it, which is the point: the Messiah came of real people with real histories, and grace did not wait for a worthier family. The genealogy is the answer to anyone who supposes his own obscure and compromised life cannot serve God's purposes.
roots_summary: Hebrew yalad means to bear or bring forth; in the causative (hiphil) stem it means to beget, and its noun toledoth gives the recurring formula these are the generations of. Greek uses gennao, whence genesis and genealogia.
roots_lines: Hebrew yalad (H3205) — to bear, bring forth; in the causative stem, to beget.
Hebrew toledoth (H8435) — generations, descendants; the structural formula that divides the book of Genesis.
Greek gennao (G1080) — to beget or bring forth; its aorist egennesen repeats through Matthew 1.
Greek genealogia (G1076) — a genealogy; Paul warns against endless genealogies used for speculation.
Saxon begitan — to get, obtain, procreate; the root of the English verb.
usage: Of the earliest recorded line of descent: Irad begat Mehujael: and Mehujael begat Methusael (Genesis 4:18).
Of the entrance of a tyrant into history: Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth (Genesis 10:8).
Of the birth of the man of promise: Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran (Genesis 11:26).

pos: v. (past tense of dig; rendering Hebrew chaphar and karah, Greek orusso)
etymology: The older regular past tense of dig, now irregular as dug. In Scripture the word divides sharply: wells are digged for life, and pits are digged for the destruction of a neighbour, and the two uses stand at opposite moral poles.
biblical_def: Digged is the older past of dig, and Scripture puts it to two opposite uses. The first is the digging of wells, which in a dry land is the making of life possible and, in the patriarchal narratives, a recurring occasion of both covenant and strife. Abraham gives Abimelech seven ewe lambs “that they may be a witness unto me, that I have digged this well” (Genesis 21:30). Isaac's servants dig, are driven off, and dig again, naming the wells for the quarrels attached to them. Even the Egyptians, when the river turned to blood, “digged round about the river for water to drink” (Exodus 7:24). The second use is the digging of pits to trap the innocent, a figure the psalmists return to repeatedly: “without cause have they hid for me their net in a pit, which without cause they have digged for my soul” (Psalm 35:7); “The proud have digged pits for me, which are not after thy law” (Psalm 119:85). Jeremiah says the same of his own townsmen (Jeremiah 18:22). The digger of wells gives; the digger of pits takes, and Scripture regularly notes that he falls into his own.
webster_summary: The older past tense of dig, now dug. Scripture divides the word sharply between the digging of wells, which gives life in a dry land, and the digging of pits, the standing figure for a trap laid against the innocent.
webster_full: DIGGED, v. The past tense and participle of dig; now more commonly dug.
2. To open or break the ground with a spade or other instrument.
3. To excavate; as, to dig a well, to dig a pit.
4. The Hebrew chaphar is to dig or search out; karah is to dig or hollow.
5. In Scripture, I have digged this well, Gen. 21; The proud have digged pits for me, Psa. 119.
corruption_summary: The pit dug for another is one of Scripture's most consistent pictures of how sin recoils on the sinner, and it names a real providence rather than a proverbial hope: the maker of mischief regularly falls into what he made.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is retributive providence — that God governs the world so that wickedness frequently destroys itself. The psalmist states it flatly: he made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made. Haman built a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai and hanged on it; Daniel's accusers were cast into the den they had contrived. This is not karma, an impersonal mechanism of moral cause and effect. It is the deliberate ordering of a personal God who judges within history as well as at the end of it.

Two cautions keep the doctrine honest. It is not invariable in this life — Psalm 73 exists precisely because the wicked often prosper and die at ease, and the psalmist is only steadied when he considers their end. And it is never a licence to gloat: Proverbs forbids rejoicing when an enemy falls. The believer's part is neither to dig pits nor to watch for others to fall into them, but to commit his cause to Him that judgeth righteously, as Christ did when He was reviled and reviled not again.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaphar is to dig or search out, and karah is to dig or hollow; both are used of wells and of pits, the moral difference lying entirely in the purpose. Greek orusso is to dig, used of the winepress and the buried talent.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaphar (H2658) — to dig, to search out; used of wells and of the spies searching the land.
Hebrew karah (H3738) — to dig or hollow out; used of the pit dug for a neighbour.
Hebrew be'er (H875) — a well; the object of the patriarchs' digging and of their disputes.
Hebrew shachath (H7845) — a pit or ditch; where the digger of mischief falls.
Greek orusso (G3736) — to dig; used of digging a winepress and of digging in the earth to hide a talent.
usage: Of a well dug and defended by covenant: that they may be a witness unto me, that I have digged this well (Genesis 21:30).
Of a trap laid without cause: without cause they have digged for my soul (Psalm 35:7).
Of the proud contriving against the godly: The proud have digged pits for me, which are not after thy law (Psalm 119:85).

And he said, For these seven ewe lambs shalt thou take of my hand, that they may be a witness unto me, that I have digged this well.
Exodus 7:24
And all the Egyptians digged round about the river for water to drink; for they could not drink of the water of the river.
Psalm 35:7
For without cause have they hid for me their net in a pit, which without cause they have digged for my soul.
Psalm 119:85
The proud have digged pits for me, which are not after thy law.

pos: v. (past tense of work; rendering Hebrew 'asah and pa'al, Greek ergazomai and katergazomai)
etymology: The older strong past tense of work, from Saxon worhte; modern English has levelled it to worked, keeping wrought only in fixed phrases such as wrought iron. In the Authorized Version it covers craftsmanship, labour, God's working, and the sea in a storm.
biblical_def: Wrought is the old past of work, and it runs from the workshop to the womb. It is the word for skilled craftsmanship in the service of God: “all the wise men, that wrought all the work of the sanctuary” (Exodus 36:4), and the labourers over whom Solomon's officers ruled at the building of the temple (1 Kings 5:16). It is the word for ordinary trade, and the apostle is not embarrassed by it: Paul lodged with Aquila and Priscilla “because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Acts 18:3). It describes the sea working itself into a storm around a fleeing prophet: “the sea wrought, and was tempestuous” (Jonah 1:11). And in the psalm it describes God's work in the hidden formation of a human body: “My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth” (Psalm 139:15) — embroidered, the Hebrew suggests, like the woven work of the tabernacle veil.
webster_summary: The older past tense of work, now levelled to worked. In Scripture it covers the craftsmen who wrought the sanctuary, the apostle who wrought at tentmaking, the sea that wrought and was tempestuous, and the body curiously wrought in secret.
webster_full: WROUGHT, v. [Sax. worhte.] The past tense and participle of work; now more commonly worked.
2. Formed by labor; manufactured; as, wrought iron, wrought silver.
3. Performed; accomplished; effected; as, God wrought a great deliverance.
4. Agitated; moved with violence; as, the sea wrought and was tempestuous.
5. In Scripture, that wrought all the work of the sanctuary, Exo. 36; curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth, Psa. 139.
corruption_summary: Psalm 139 describes God at work in the unborn body, and the passage settles the question modern law will not settle: the child in the womb is a person known, formed, and written in God's book before he is seen by anyone else.
corruption_paragraphs: The psalm does not argue the case; it assumes it and worships. Thou hast covered me in my mother's womb; my substance was not hid from thee; thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written. The continuity of the pronoun is the argument: the me being formed in secret is the same me who now writes the psalm. Scripture nowhere marks a point at which a developing human becomes a person; Jeremiah was known before he was formed, and John leaped in Elisabeth's womb at the greeting of Mary.

The word curiously wrought is worth pausing on. The Hebrew verb is used of the embroiderer's work in the tabernacle — the skilled, deliberate, many-coloured needlework of the veil and the hangings. The psalmist reaches for a craftsman's image because he is describing a craftsman's act, done in the dark and at leisure and with attention. What follows for the church is not only opposition to the destruction of such life but the corresponding duty: care for mothers in distress, for the fatherless, and for children nobody wants, since the God who wrought them in secret has not stopped attending to them.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'asah is to do or make, pa'al is to work or accomplish, and raqam is to embroider — the verb of Psalm 139:15. Greek ergazomai is to work, and katergazomai to work out or accomplish fully.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'asah (H6213) — to do, make, fashion; the general verb of both divine and human work.
Hebrew pa'al (H6466) — to work, to accomplish; often of a deliberate and finished action.
Hebrew raqam (H7551) — to embroider or variegate; the curiously wrought of Psalm 139:15, used also of the tabernacle hangings.
Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to work, to labour, to trade; used of Paul at his tentmaking.
Greek katergazomai (G2716) — to work out, accomplish thoroughly; work out your own salvation.
usage: Of skilled craftsmen serving the sanctuary: all the wise men, that wrought all the work of the sanctuary (Exodus 36:4).
Of an apostle supporting himself by a trade: he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers (Acts 18:3).
Of God's hidden work in forming a body: curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth (Psalm 139:15).
scriptures: Exodus 36:4
And all the wise men, that wrought all the work of the sanctuary, came every man from his work which they made;
Psalm 139:15
My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth.
Acts 18:3
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
Jonah 1:11
Then said they unto him, What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous.

pos: v. (past tense of bear; rendering Hebrew yalad and nasa', Greek eteken and emarturesen); distinguish the adjective bare, naked
etymology: The older past tense of bear, now bore. English bear itself has two great senses — to bring forth a child, and to carry a burden — and the Authorized Version uses bare for both. The adjective bare, meaning naked or uncovered, is an unrelated word.
biblical_def: Bare is the old past of bear, and it carries two of the weightiest ideas in Scripture. In the sense of childbearing it records the first birth in human history: “she conceived, and bare Cain, and said, I have gotten a man from the LORD” (Genesis 4:1). It records Leah's fourth son and the turn in her heart that named him: “she conceived again, and bare a son: and she said, Now will I praise the LORD; therefore she called his name Judah” — the tribe of the Messiah named out of a woman's praise after years of being unloved. In the sense of carrying, the verb bears the whole doctrine of substitution: the Servant “bare the sin of many”, and Peter writes that He “bare our sins in his own body on the tree”. And in a third sense the word is used of testimony — to bear witness: “Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth” (John 5:33). Childbirth, burden-bearing, and witness are three different things in English; in the biblical languages they are close enough that the same English verb serves.
webster_summary: The older past tense of bear, now bore; used both of bringing forth a child and of carrying a burden, and in the phrase bare witness. Distinguish the adjective bare, naked or uncovered.
webster_full: BARE, v. The past tense of bear; now more commonly bore.
2. To bring forth, as a child; as, she bare a son.
3. To carry; to sustain; to support a weight or a burden; as, he bare our sins.
4. BARE, a. [Sax. bær.] Naked; uncovered; destitute of covering. A distinct word.
5. In Scripture, she conceived, and bare Cain, Gen. 4; he bare witness unto the truth, John 5.
corruption_summary: The bearing of sin by a substitute is the doctrine most persistently attacked in modern theology, dismissed as cosmic child abuse or as a crude legalism. Scripture presents it as the heart of the gospel and the Father's own will, willingly embraced by the Son.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection charges that penal substitution makes the Father a punisher of the innocent, and it fails at two points. First, the Son is not a third party dragged into another's quarrel: He is God, and He gives Himself — no man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. The Trinity is not divided at Calvary; the Father sends, the Son offers, and the Spirit sustains. Second, the transaction is not unjust because the Substitute is willing and the union real: Christ is joined to His people as head to body, and He may therefore lawfully answer for them.

Isaiah 53 states the exchange with a precision no other passage matches: the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all; he was wounded for our transgressions; he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors. Peter puts it in the past tense and locates it exactly: who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree. Every attempt to replace this with a merely exemplary or governmental account leaves the guilt unanswered and the conscience unrelieved. It is precisely because the burden was borne that it is not still ours to carry.
roots_summary: Hebrew yalad is to bear a child and nasa' is to lift or carry, including the carrying of guilt; Greek tikto is to bring forth and anaphero to bear up, the verb of 1 Peter 2:24. Martureo gives bare witness.
roots_lines: Hebrew yalad (H3205) — to bear or bring forth a child; the verb of Genesis 4:1.
Hebrew nasa' (H5375) — to lift, carry, bear; used of bearing iniquity, both by the sinner and by the substitute.
Hebrew sabal (H5445) — to bear a heavy load; he shall bear their iniquities in Isaiah 53:11.
Greek anaphero (G399) — to carry up, to offer; bare our sins in his own body on the tree.
Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness, to testify; the sense in John 5:33.
usage: Of the first birth recorded in Scripture: she conceived, and bare Cain (Genesis 4:1).
Of the naming of Judah out of praise: she conceived again, and bare a son... therefore she called his name Judah (Genesis 29:35).
Of testimony given to the truth: Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth (John 5:33).
scriptures: Genesis 44:27
And thy servant my father said unto us, Ye know that my wife bare me two sons:
John 5:33
Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth.
2 Samuel 12:15
And Nathan departed unto his house. And the LORD struck the child that Uriah's wife bare unto David, and it was very sick.
Jeremiah 22:26
And I will cast thee out, and thy mother that bare thee, into another country, where ye were not born; and there shall ye die.

pos: v. (the Authorized Version's spelling of show; rendering Hebrew ra'ah in the causative and 'asah, Greek deiknumi)
etymology: An older spelling of show, pronounced the same, from Saxon sceawian, to look at or display. The Authorized Version spells it shew throughout, which is why the table in the tabernacle is the table of shewbread — the bread of the presence, set out where God could see it.
biblical_def: Shew is the Authorized Version's spelling of show, and it covers both what God displays and what men are commanded to display. God's call to Abram is built on it, and on a deliberate withholding: “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee” (Genesis 12:1). The land is not named. Abram must leave everything before he learns where he is going, and Hebrews notes that he went out not knowing whither he went. The psalmist asks for the same kind of showing in the moral realm: “Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths” (Psalm 25:4). The prophets turn the verb toward conduct: “Execute true judgment, and shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother” (Zechariah 7:9), and Isaiah's bracing summons, “Remember this, and shew yourselves men” (Isaiah 46:8). And Christ promises that the Spirit will shew His disciples what belongs to Him: “he shall take of mine, and shall shew it unto you” (John 16:15).
webster_summary: The Authorized Version's spelling of show: to display, to make known, to point out. In Scripture it is used of the land God would shew Abram, the ways the psalmist asks to be shewn, and the mercy men are commanded to shew one another.
webster_full: SHEW, v.t. [Sax. sceawian, to look at.] To exhibit or present to view; to display. The older spelling of show.
2. To make known; to reveal; to teach; as, shew me thy ways.
3. To bestow; to confer; as, to shew mercy, to shew kindness.
4. SHEWBREAD, n. The bread set every sabbath before the Lord on the table in the sanctuary.
5. In Scripture, unto a land that I will shew thee, Gen. 12; shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother, Zech. 7.
corruption_summary: Guidance is now widely sought as advance information — a map of the future disclosed before obedience begins. God's dealing with Abram runs the other way: the going comes first, and the shewing follows.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is that God's revealed will is for obedience and His secret will is not ours to inspect. Abram is told to leave and is not told where he will arrive; the land is a land that I will shew thee, future tense, and Hebrews commends him precisely for going out not knowing. Deuteronomy 29:29 draws the line: the secret things belong unto the LORD our God, but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children, that we may do all the words of this law.

A great deal of Christian anxiety about guidance is the attempt to cross that line — to obtain, before acting, the information God has reserved. Psalm 25:4 shows the prayer Scripture actually models: Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths, a request for the character of God's ways rather than a preview of events. The believer is furnished for every decision by the commandments, by wisdom, and by counsel, and is not promised more. What remains hidden is not withheld unkindly; it is the difference between a creature and his Maker, and accepting it is most of what trust means.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'ah in the causative stem means to cause to see, to shew; 'asah chesed is to do or shew mercy. Greek deiknumi is to point out or exhibit, and anadeiknumi to display openly.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see; in the causative stem, to cause to see, to shew.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant mercy, lovingkindness; what men are commanded to shew one another in Zechariah 7:9.
Hebrew lechem happanim (H3899, H6440) — the bread of the faces or of the presence; the shewbread of the sanctuary.
Greek deiknumi (G1166) — to shew, point out, exhibit; used of the Spirit shewing the things of Christ.
Saxon sceawian — to look at, to behold; the root of both shew and show.
usage: Of a call obeyed before the destination is known: unto a land that I will shew thee (Genesis 12:1).
Of prayer for the character of God's ways: Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths (Psalm 25:4).
Of mercy required between brethren: shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother (Zechariah 7:9).
scriptures: Genesis 12:1
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
Psalm 25:4
Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths.
Zechariah 7:9
Thus speaketh the LORD of hosts, saying, Execute true judgment, and shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother:
Isaiah 46:8
